https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The embrace of Russia by Niger, and other Sahel states, has been seen as a rejection of the post-colonial Western powers By Simi Jolaoso Africa correspondent Published 5 hours ago When mutinous soldiers seized a strategic military base in Niger's capital last Saturday, the country's ruling junta turned to a foreign partner it has increasingly relied on since coming to power: Russia. Following a night of intense fighting in Niamey, Russia's Africa Corps helped Nigerien loyalist forces to regain control of Air Base 101 at Diori Hamani International Airport. Africa Corps, unlike its predecessor the Wagner Group, is directly under the control of the defence ministry in Moscow. It provides combat support and military training and is thought to have some 200 to 300 men in Niger. Russia's ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropaev, publicly acknowledged the weekend intervention, saying his country's forces had helped "repress a mutiny". "This is seen as a symbolic victory," according to Beverly Ochieng, senior analyst at Control Risks. "[One] that will continue to put them at the centre of not just the counter-insurgency campaign, but even in the protection and prolongation of military rule." The attempted coup offers perhaps the clearest evidence yet that Africa Corps' role in three Sahel countries extends beyond its stated mission of helping governments fight jihadist insurgencies. Russia is increasingly demonstrating that it can provide something perhaps even more valuable to the military rulers of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso: protection for the governments themselves. Image source, APTN Image caption, After the mutiny was put down, state television broadcast images of the arrest of some of the soliders "It was not sufficient to bring stability," said Ochieng, "but it's enough to allow these military governments to have a political lifeline." The thwarted mutiny also highlights something the ruling junta may not want to admit - just how dependent on Moscow it has become for security. In January, Africa Corps personnel also played an important role in repelling an attack at the same airport. "We saw videos of the jihadists walking around the airport basically completely unimpeded," said Jacob Boswall, a security analyst who tracks jihadist activity for the BBC's media monitoring service. "Probably there is some substance to the claim that Africa Corps was able to restore power in that case [in January]. And I think, again, in this case as well, that intervention was very significant." One of the Nigerien military's central justifications for the July 2023 coup, which saw Gen Abdourahamane Tiani seize power, was the deteriorating security situation and alleged failure of Niger's civilian authorities, under elected President Mohamed Bazoum, to tackle it. They also blamed Western partners at the time for their inability to contain jihadist violence. Yet, three years later, that insurgency remains unresolved. Militants linked to al-Qaeda and Islamic State have continued to launch attacks, including in the TillabÃ©ri and Dosso regions. Some, inflicting heavy casualties on security forces. Ochieng described this latest mutiny as evidence of longstanding grievances within Niger's own military, compounded by the pressure the soldiers have been facing. "Counter-insurgency forces do not feel adequately supported by the military government," she said. "There have been challenges in providing equipment and replenishments." Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, On Wednesday, soldiers appeared at a pro-junta rally in the capital, Niamey Niger's government is facing threats on two fronts: extremist militant groups attacking the state, and grievances within its armed forces responsible for fighting them. Africa Corps may have helped contain the latter this past weekend, but it has yet to resolve the former. Unlike Wagner mercenaries, whose status in a private military company allowed Moscow some deniability, Africa Corps is more clearly an instrument of the Russian state. "The whole point of Africa Corps is that it brings the power back under the control of the Russian Ministry of Defence," said Boswall. Officially, its forces are deployed to help Sahel governments combat Islamist militant groups. But dissidents contemplating moves against military governments elsewhere in the Sahel region may now have to factor Russian forces into their calculations. Despite the struggle to contain the jihadists, no-one anticipates Africa Corps leaving the Sahel any time soon. Keeping those governments in power protects Russia's investment. "Wagner - and now Africa Corps - have always had a very transactional interest in Africa," Boswall said. "If they can get mineral resources in exchange for providing protection and defence, then they will. We see that in Mali with goldâ¦ and then in Niger, it really is uranium [that] seems to be the main resource that Africa Corps is protecting." Analysts say Russia also benefits from having friendly governments that could support it in international forums. "Having that kind of international group of supportive countries, Russia sees as giving Russia credibility - diplomatic credibility," Boswall explained. Like Mali and Burkina Faso, Tiani's government has built much of its legitimacy using the language of sovereignty, pan-Africanism and liberation from former colonial powers. All three governments ordered French troops to leave. They also formed the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) and subsequently withdrew from the West African regional bloc Ecowas, presenting the new alliance as an assertion of regional independence. Some analysts regard this as at odds with its growing reliance on Africa Corps. "The military governments argue that they have selected Russia on their own terms," said Ochieng. "Russia is seen as a partner that respects that sovereignty, unlike their previous partnerships with France or even the EU and, to some extent, with the US." Image source, Reuters Image caption, Niger's Gen Abdourahamane Tiani (C), Mali's Gen Assimi GoÃ¯ta (L) and Burkina Faso's Capt Ibrahim TraorÃ© (R) came together for the first heads of state summit of the AES in 2024 An army captain on Niger state television accused foreign powers, including France and Chad, of being behind last weekend's unrest, while Russia's foreign ministry described the mutineers as "extremists seemingly incited by European former colonial powers". France has repeatedly rejected accusations that it is attempting to destabilise Niger. Chad's government did not respond to a BBC request for comment. "[Niger is] underplaying the role that Africa Corps has in these countries, and they're overplaying the resource-nationalism narrative - the idea that the government is in control and fighting back against the jihadists," explained Boswall. "There is a huge media war going on in the Sahel to control the narrative around that." Russia's war with Ukraine is another important factor shaping its strategy in the Sahel. The conflict continues to consume Russian personnel and military equipment, limiting how far Moscow can expand its operations in Africa. "It's quite a tightrope for Russia because ultimately its priority will always be Ukraine," Ochieng said. "It will maintain at least enough numbers to allow it to reassure the military governments in the Sahel that it continues to be a reliable partner. They'll continue to deploy just enough weapons and supplies and logisticsâ¦ to continue supporting Africa Corps." But there are limits to what that support can achieve. "Russia cannot afford a sustained counter-offensive anywhere in the Sahel," Ochieng said. This may help explain why protecting allied governments appears to have become such an important part of Russia's regional strategy. Defending a capital or helping loyalist forces defeat a mutiny requires fewer resources than recapturing and securing vast areas affected by an insurgency. "These are quite limited interventions, but with an outsized impact," Boswall said. "I think at that level they'll be able to sustain that over the foreseeable future, even with the war in Ukraine." Russia may have helped Tiani survive this latest security challenge, but it has not removed the conditions that could produce the next mutiny. https://www.politico.eu/article/le-canad.text: BRUXELLES — La proposition d’Ursula von der Leyen de faire du Canada le “premier membre associé” de l’UE a surpris les Etats membres, et suscité des inquiétudes quant aux contreparties que cela pourrait impliquer. Lors de son discours annuel sur l’état de l’Union prononcé à Strasbourg mercredi, la présidente de la Commission européenne a suggéré d’“élever les relations avec le Canada au plus au niveau possible”, considérant qu’il est “urgent de réinventer nos partenariats” et de “construire des coalitions mondiales pour assurer notre résilience et préserver nos démocraties”. Mais ce message a pris au dépourvu les gouvernements européens, qui n’avaient jamais été invités à se prononcer sur cette idée avant le discours, affirment trois diplomates ayant souhaité garder l’anonymat afin de pouvoir s’exprimer librement. L’adhésion à l’UE relève de la compétence du Conseil européen, et il n’existe pas de statut de membre associé. Advertisement Advertisement “Personne ne sait vraiment ce que cela signifie”, pointe l’un de ces diplomates, qui a participé ces derniers jours à des discussions avec la Commission au sujet des relations avec le Canada. “Les Etats membres ont tenté de tempérer les attentes. Ottawa suscite beaucoup de sympathie, mais nous devons connaître les détails.” Un deuxième diplomate s’est exprimé sans détour : le Canada pourrait au mieux se voir proposer l’équivalent d’une zone de libre-échange approfondi et complet (ZLEAC) — un dispositif donnant accès au marché européen, dont profitent la Géorgie, la Moldavie et l’Ukraine —, car il y a peu de soutien pour une autre forme d’intégration économique ou politique. “Les Etats membres ne s’accorderont sur rien d’autre”, anticipe-t-il. Un troisième diplomate a ajouté que tout statut de membre associé nécessiterait des modifications des traités fondamentaux de l’UE — ce qui est “impossible”, car le nombre de soutiens est insuffisant. Un processus qui soulèverait un tas de questions Parmi les problèmes potentiels qui pourraient surgir s’ils envisageaient d’aller plus loin, selon les diplomates, figurent : des questions épineuses liées à la préférence d’Ottawa pour le made in Canada , qui pourrait aller à l’encontre des règles du marché unique ; l’industrie sidérurgique canadienne, qui rivalise avec celle de l’Europe ; la taxation des exportations automobiles de l’UE et les règles limitant les importations d’alcool européen ; ainsi que des positions divergentes concernant les OGM. Le chancelier allemand Friedrich Merz avait précédemment proposé le statut de “membre associé” comme moyen d’approfondir le rapprochement avec l’Ukraine , mais cette idée a été rejetée par Kyiv et n’a pas réussi à rallier le soutien des autres dirigeants européens. Les ambassadeurs de l’ensemble de l’UE ont rencontré la Commission et le Conseil européen la semaine dernière, où ils se sont globalement mis d’accord sur l’idée de resserrer les liens avec le Canada. Et même ceux représentant des gouvernements de droite, habituellement plus prudents par crainte de s’attirer les foudres du président Donald Trump, alors qu’Ottawa est engagé dans une guerre commerciale de plus en plus intense avec les Etats-Unis. Advertisement Advertisement En réaction à l’annonce d’Ursula von der Leyen, le ministre irlandais des Affaires européennes, Thomas Byrne, a déclaré que “l’élargissement de notre Union à des membres à part entière, et peut-être à des membres associés, relève de notre intérêt stratégique”. Mais les députés européens présents dans l’hémicycle se sont montrés moins convaincus. L’élue française Insoumise Manon Aubry a ainsi interpelé Ursula von der Leyen : “Qui vous a donné un mandat démocratique et populaire pour cela ?” Le Premier ministre canadien Mark Carney a assisté à ce discours dans le cadre d’un déplacement, comme l’avait révélé POLITICO . Face aux menaces commerciales et politiques de Washington, il a plaidé pour que son pays mette fin à sa dépendance aux Etats-Unis et pour la formation d’un club de démocraties partageant les mêmes valeurs et favorables au libre-échange. Cette visite avait pour but “de signaler clairement l’intention et l’ambition des deux parties de renforcer notre partenariat”, avait déclaré à l’époque un haut responsable de l’UE. Jeudi, Mark Carney exposera sa propre vision de l’avenir des relations entre l’Union et le Canada lors d’un discours devant le Parlement européen. Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

http://www.russiaherald.com/news/2793026.text: Lukashenko vows Belarus army shake-up amid mobiilsation warning RT.com 11 Sep 2026, 22:25 GMT+10 Minsk seeks to shake up its military and get it ready for a potential war, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko has said Belarus will bolster its military combat readiness and could even announce "mobilization" to test it, President Alexander Lukashenko has said. The Belarusian leader made the remarks on Friday when he toured the Obuz-Lesnovsky military training grounds near the city of Baranovichi in the west of the country. During his visit, Lukashenko met top military officials and inspected communications and control systems. The president said that he was set to continue vetting the country's forces, revealing that an artillery brigade and signal troops are currently undergoing extensive inspections. "I've already put it in plain terms: the army needs a shake-up - the time has come. The entire army. We will vet everyone. Right up to the point of mobilization," Lukashenko told reporters. The vetting process is set to be as close to real war conditions as possible, he added. "We are preparing for war so that it does not happen," the Belarusian leader stated. Speaking to senior military officials, the president reiterated that Minsk was not seeking to attack anyone but only to bolster its defenses. "We have no intention of attacking anyone; we are pragmatists. We understand that attacking anyone - say, one of our neighbors - would be tantamount to suicide. We cannot win a conflict against the 'monsters' - the states situated along our borders," he said. While it was not immediately clear which countries exactly Lukashenko described as "monsters," most of the Belarusian neighbors' militaries greatly surpass its capabilities. Minsk maintains a modestly sized military of less than 50,000 active-duty servicemen, against some 1.5 million troops in Belarus' key ally, Russia. Ukraine, which has been locked in a conflict with Russia for over four years, is believed to have around 900,000 active-duty personnel. Other neighbors of Belarus, Poland, Lithuania, and Latvia are NATO member states. While the two Baltic nations have tiny militaries, Warsaw has been actively building up its force recently. Poland has some 220,000 active-duty troops and continues to expand the force as well as rearm it with modern weaponry. Numbers-wise, the country's military has become the third-largest within the NATO bloc, surpassed only by the US and Türkiye. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan attends a press conference following a meeting between Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan in Istanbul on Aug. 31. Yasin Akgul/AFP via Getty Images Military October 6, 2026, 4:18 PM Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at joint efforts to counter Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia , the potential future of nuclear weapons in Lithuania , and espionage allegations against a former German spy chief. Joint Deterrence Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey triggered a mutual defense pact on Monday in response to repeated Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure. The joint deterrence measures, which appear to include the “rapid deployment” of Pakistani and Turkish troops to the Persian Gulf kingdom, mark the first time that the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement has been invoked since it was signed in August. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at joint efforts to counter Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia , the potential future of nuclear weapons in Lithuania , and espionage allegations against a former German spy chief. Joint Deterrence Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey triggered a mutual defense pact on Monday in response to repeated Houthi strikes on Saudi infrastructure. The joint deterrence measures, which appear to include the “rapid deployment” of Pakistani and Turkish troops to the Persian Gulf kingdom, mark the first time that the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement has been invoked since it was signed in August. The Houthis have yet to comment on the activation of the mutual defense pact. Under the trilateral, NATO-style agreement , “any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” Although military cooperation among the three Sunni Muslim-majority nations is nothing new, the timing of the pact’s creation was particularly notable, as it came less than one month after Yemen’s Houthi rebels began launching attacks on Saudi Arabia. In recent weeks, fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government has only worsened. Houthi forces seized control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait, and targeted critical energy infrastructure and Muslim holy sites in Saudi Arabia. This week, the Houthis also claimed to have launched attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia’s Aramco-associated Petro Rabigh refinery, and other locations. In response, Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen launched a counteroffensive on Monday in an effort to retake the coastal territory. Yemeni officials said the forces successfully recaptured several key towns near Bab el-Mandeb. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has doubled down on the defense of its own territory by bringing Pakistan and Turkey further into the fold. A joint statement released by the three countries following Monday’s emergency meeting in Riyadh did not explicitly name the Houthis as the rationale for activating the pact, though it did cite recent attacks on the holy cities of Mecca and Medina. It is unclear to what extent Islamabad and Ankara will aid Riyadh. The trio announced on Monday that they will “move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.” However, Pakistan said it will not release the details of its deployment, though Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif said on Monday that Islamabad and Ankara were already aiding Riyadh in a “ supporting role ,” including in the form of reconnaissance. And the Turkish parliament has yet to ratify the mutual defense pact. Still, even the threat of joint involvement could dramatically shift the Saudi-Houthi conflict. The members of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement boast a combined military strength of nearly 1.4 million active troops. That doesn’t include their 3,400 aircraft, 6,000 tanks, and more than 340 naval assets. Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority nation in the world, and Turkey has NATO’s second-largest armed forces . Lithuania’s parliament voted in favor of a constitutional amendment on Tuesday that would lift a ban on nuclear weapons being stationed on the country’s soil. “With the current restriction, we cannot fully participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans,” opposition leader Laurynas Kasciunas said. “Since nuclear deterrence is the queen of all deterrence, this decision is strategically important,” he added. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas echoed that rationale, arguing that if “Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions that we are having today.” Article 137 of the Lithuanian Constitution prohibits the country from hosting nuclear weapons or foreign military bases on its territory. Tuesday’s amendment would only reverse the nuclear weapons ban, though U.S. President Donald Trump has recently proposed building a U.S. military base in Lithuania. Two ballots are required to pass for any change to take effect; the second vote is scheduled for Jan. 12. Moscow did not take the news lightly. On Tuesday, Russia warned Lithuania that altering Article 137 to allow for nuclear weapons or a NATO base deployment would spark greater conflict in the region. “Neither of these developments will contribute to stability and predictability on the European continent,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday. “On the contrary, they will, to our regret, mark yet another significant escalation of tensions.” Espionage allegations. German police arrested former spy chief August Hanning on Tuesday on suspicion of espionage, disclosure of state secrets, attempted treason, and working as a secret service agent. It is unclear which foreign government German authorities believe that Hanning allegedly helped. A former chief of staff to one of Hanning’s successors was also arrested on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and espionage against the state.” Germany’s federal prosecutor’s office alleges that the man, identified only as Manfred D., provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 government documents, many of which were classified, in the years after Hanning had left his post. Hanning served as the head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, from 1998 to 2005, after which he worked for the Federal Interior Ministry and eventually moved into the private sector as a consultant. He is the first former head of Germany’s intelligence agency to be accused of espionage . Hanning, who has denied the allegations, and Manfred D. are expected to appear before a judge later this week; Manfred D. has yet to comment on the charges. Tuesday’s revelations come amid another scandal for Hanning. Evidence of the spy chief’s alleged actions was only discovered during a separate, unrelated investigation into a German steakhouse heiress who is on trial for the attempted kidnapping of her children from her estranged husband. Prosecutors in that case allege that Hanning helped connect the woman to the Israeli spy firm that is accused of carrying out the abduction; Hanning has denied any involvement in the kidnapping. His work as a consultant has also come under scrutiny in the past. Growing Ebola outbreak. Kenya recorded its first case of Ebola on Tuesday, expanding the deadly outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo into East Africa. According to local authorities, the man—a Kenyan national who had lived in Congo for the past seven years—became ill last month, traveled into Uganda via road, and then flew to Nairobi on Saturday. He died at a private hospital in the Kenyan capital late Monday. Congo confirmed its first case of Ebola’s rare Bundibugyo strand on May 15. Since then, more than 8,400 cases have been reported, making this year’s outbreak the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic in the country’s history. Already, Ebola deaths in Congo have surpassed 4,000. Uganda and France have also recorded Ebola cases, though only three deaths have been confirmed outside of Congo—the third being this week’s incident in Kenya. Congo’s neighbors have implemented strict travel restrictions to prevent the virus’s spread. Uganda closed its border with Congo in May, and Kenya has required all travelers from Congo to fill out an online questionnaire about their potential exposure and health status before being granted entry. This week’s case in Nairobi “underscores the importance of sustained preparedness across the region,” the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said in a statement . Odds and Ends This year’s Nobel Prize in physics went to Francis Halzen on Tuesday for his work pioneering a new type of astronomy known as neutrino astronomy. In the late 1980s, Halzen conceptualized using light sensors embedded deep within the South Pole’s ice to detect high-energy neutrinos originating from the distant cosmos. That work eventually led to the development of the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, where Halzen and more than 400 researchers from around the world use the information from the telescope to understand more about the inner workings of phenomena such as supermassive black holes.
